concepts.title: Robustness and Generalization in Vision Systems
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision systems gain robustness and generalization by training on diverse data, allowing them to handle conditions that break fragile, hand-crafted models.
concepts.content:
Transitioning from hand-crafted systems to neural networks allows for 3D interpretation without manually detecting edges or features. The neural network learns to compute the features it deems necessary to solve the task. While a learned-based model might lose some local accuracy—such as recovering a ground plane as concave rather than flat or producing twisted cube faces—it gains significantly in robustness and generalization.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using a pretrained model. The images show multiple view points of the reconstructed 3D scene from @fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1)

Hand-crafted approaches can produce precise results when images fit their specific world assumptions, but they are fragile. Poor illumination or a simple change in the scene, like changing the ground color, can break edge detectors and cause a cascade of errors. Conversely, learning-based approaches like MiDaS produce results of consistent quality regardless of conditions. 

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

(see figure: Out of domain generalization. For the pretrained model, these images might still be within the domain of the training, as it contained a very diverse set of natural images. The simple system model...)

While hand-crafted models offer a comprehensive understanding of their own mechanisms and require no training data, they do not generalize outside the space defined by their assumptions. Pretrained systems are able to deal with configurations that were not part of the original modeling assumptions and are robust to changes in illumination. Even though these networks do not rely on explicit hand-coded heuristics, they may still be performing equivalent operations internally, as 3D information is fundamentally contained in edges and junctions.
concepts.motivation_md: Hand-crafted vision systems are often brittle, failing when lighting changes or assumptions are slightly violated. This concept explores how deep learning models trade perfect geometric precision for the ability to function reliably across diverse, unpredictable real-world environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Hand-crafted models are precise under strict assumptions but fragile to environmental changes like lighting or color.

concepts.title: LLM-based Scene Understanding
concepts.one_liner: Large Language Models like GPT-4v can interpret and reason about the 3D geometry of scenes by leveraging massive training data and transformer architectures.
concepts.content:
Large Language Models, such as GPT-4v, provide an alternative for interpreting visual scenes by allowing users to ask questions about images. This method is remarkably accurate because the underlying transformer, trained on massive data, may have learned rules equivalent to detecting edges, using wavelet-like filters, and reasoning about perspective geometry to estimate shape.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

However, scene understanding is not yet fully solved. While GPT-4v can recognize geometric figures and their spatial configurations, the integration with rendering engines remains fragile. For example, attempting to reconstruct or re-render an image from the model's text description often results in errors or inconsistencies.

(see figure: Output by ChatGPT when asked to render a new image with the same elements as in @fig-chatgpt_blockworld This conversation is a continuation of the same chat from @fig-chatgpt_blockworld)

[FIGURE:2d5b0345de81fa09]

These failures provide clues to the next fundamental questions in computer vision, such as how to better integrate high-level recognition with precise geometric rendering.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional vision systems often struggle with semantic context. LLMs offer a way to combine visual recognition with high-level reasoning, though they still face challenges in perfectly translating that understanding back into precise 3D reconstructions.

concepts.title: Unsolved Solved Computer Vision Problems
concepts.one_liner: In computer vision, many seemingly 'solved' problems are actually illusions that mask deeper, underlying challenges requiring creative new directions.
concepts.content:
Computer vision is making amazing progress, but it is important to be wary of "unsolved solved computer vision problems." For certain tasks, it may appear as if a single method has perfectly resolved the issue or that foundational problems are fully addressed. However, this is often an illusion; the problem may not be truly solved, and many unsolved problems typically lurk in the background of every perceived success.

Advances in the field are the result of exploring new directions with an open mind and using creativity as a tool. The precise answers to current questions are less important than the ability to challenge existing approaches and identify relevant questions for new systems. With the rise of learning-based systems, researchers find themselves performing experiments similar to psychophysics to understand the internal mechanisms of these artificial visual systems.

[FIGURE:a9cf6077c82fad75]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept encourages a critical mindset, reminding students that 'state-of-the-art' solutions often have hidden limitations and that the field advances by questioning what is currently accepted as solved.
concepts.recap_md: - Many foundational problems in computer vision are only partially solved despite appearing finished.

key_passage.text: For some vision task, it might appear as if there is one method that perfectly resolves the task. It might appear as if some foundational problems in computer vision are solved. It might often seem as if it is not possible to make progress regarding certain questions. But more often than not, it is just an illusion, and the solved problem was not really solved at all.

motivation.text: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but beware of the unsolved solved computer vision problems. And even when a problem was genuinely solved (and probably is not), it's important to remember that for every solved problem, there are many unsolved problems lurking in the background.

concepts.title: Pretrained end-to-end vision systems
concepts.one_liner: Large-scale pretrained vision systems can solve complex tasks out-of-the-box, though bridging the gap to truly robust systems remains a challenge.
concepts.content: Modern computer vision embraces the use of large-scale pretrained models that can solve diverse tasks such as natural language processing, image generation, and object classification. These models, including DALL-E, GPT, and AutoPilot, are trained on massive datasets across diverse domains to improve generalization. They can be used as standalone systems with little fine-tuning or as building blocks within more complex architectures. While these systems produce astonishing results, a close analysis suggests there is still a gap to bridge to build truly reliable and robust systems. This approach revisits simple-world problems by applying high-performing, out-of-the-box pretrained models rather than relying solely on hand-crafted algorithms.
concepts.motivation_md: Pretrained models leverage massive computation and data to solve problems that were previously handled by fragile, hand-coded algorithms, offering a more generalizable approach to vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Pretrained models like DALL-E and GPT can be used with little to no fine-tuning.

concepts.title: Revisiting the simple world
concepts.one_liner: Revisiting the simple world involves recovering 3D scene structure from a single image using both first principles and modern pretrained models.
concepts.content: The goal of analyzing the simple world is to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of a scene from a single image (see figure: Image from the simple world.). This process involves deriving an algorithm from first principles: studying image formation, identifying where information is preserved, building a representation to make that information explicit, and integrating evidence to recover the 3D data lost during the image formation process.
concepts.motivation_md: By returning to a simplified environment, we can compare traditional algorithmic approaches based on physics and geometry with modern deep learning methods.
concepts.recap_md: - The primary goal is recovering 3D structure from a 2D image.

concepts.title: MiDaS
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art neural network trained end-to-end to solve 3D perception and depth estimation from single images.
concepts.content: MiDaS is a state-of-the-art pretrained model designed to solve the 3D perception problem from single images. It is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images containing ground truth depth information, as well as stereo images. From a user's perspective, the system functions as a simple function call, though effectively using it out-of-the-box requires understanding its training, its output format, and how it can be adapted to specific tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: MiDaS provides a high-performance, ready-to-use solution for depth estimation, sparing developers from building complex geometric reconstruction pipelines from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - MiDaS is an end-to-end neural network for single-image depth estimation.

key_passage.text: The current state of the art is MiDaS. The system is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images that had ground truth depth information and also using stereo images.

concepts.title: MiDaS training and invariant loss
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS uses an invariant loss during training to handle ambiguities in scale and camera parameters across diverse datasets.
concepts.content:
### How Was It Trained?

This model has been trained using a mix of four datasets with real images. (see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022) As the model is trained with a diverse collection of data sources, there is an ambiguity on the overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. Therefore, the loss is defined in a way that it can be invariant to all those ambiguities. The invariant loss makes the training more robust, but it also makes the output less convenient to use. To deal with these ambiguities, the model is trained to predict disparity (inverse depth up to scale and shift). This means that we cannot directly use the output; we need to convert it first into world coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Using diverse datasets improves generalization but introduces inconsistencies in scale; an invariant loss allows the model to learn from these varied sources without being confused by different camera setups.
concepts.recap_md: - MiDaS predicts disparity, which is inverse depth up to an unknown scale and shift.

concepts.title: Converting disparity to world coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Converting disparity to world coordinates requires inverting the disparity value and applying intrinsic and extrinsic camera matrices.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw disparity maps from neural networks lack physical scale and orientation; this technique maps those relative values into a meaningful 3D coordinate system for spatial reasoning.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth $z$ is calculated as the inverse of disparity plus a constant $d_0$.

key_passage.text: To translate the returned disparity for a given pixel $d\left[n,m \right]$ into depth values $z\left[n,m \right]$, we need to invert the disparity after adding the constant: $z \left[n,m \right] = \frac{1}{ d \left[n,m \right] + d_0}$. Now we need to recover the world coordinates for every pixel. Assuming a pinhole camera and using the depth $z \left[n,m \right]$ and the camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$, we obtain the 3D coordinates for a pixel with image coordinates $(n,m)$ in the camera reference frame as, $\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = z\left[n,m \right] \times \mathbf{K}^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} n \\ m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

motivation.text: MiDaS returns disparity values, up to an unknown constant ($d_0$), but what we need are world coordinates ($X,Y,Z$) for each pixel.

concepts.title: Camera Tilt Angle (theta)
concepts.one_liner: The camera tilt angle $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane.
concepts.content: The parameter $\theta$ represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. While it is possible to estimate this angle accurately by determining the surface normal of pixels on the ground and measuring the angle relative to the vertical axis, a simpler approach for many applications is to set it to a heuristic value. For instance, setting $\theta = \pi / 4$ is often sufficient as it approximately matches the angle at which many handheld or tripod-mounted pictures are taken.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowing the tilt of the camera is essential for correctly orienting the reconstructed 3D scene relative to the ground.
concepts.recap_md: - $\theta$ is the angle between the camera's optical axis and the ground.
